Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The author uses brief exposition and summary at the beginning to establish the burned chair, the narrator's four-month unemployment, and their habit of walking routes. It also uses summary effectively to compress time—such as the eight-block walk in the rain and the long walk home at the end. Meanwhile, the core emotional weight and climax of the story unfold in vivid, real-time scenes: spotting the couple at the crosswalk, pausing while the man ties his shoe, watching the couple prepare dinner through the lit window as the street floods, and witnessing the eerie arrival of the floating chair at their stoop. This balance keeps the pacing smooth while ensuring the central moments feel immediate and haunting.
